title: Sita's jewel
hook: a hair jewel, a story only Rama would know, and a month on the clock: the beautiful book comes to rest
carry: shravana: hearing the story again is devotion

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman put seen first, so Rama's fear was answered before the story began. Your line: vak tapas, speech that's true, kind and calming.

Hanuman has told the story. Now he opens his hand. In it is a jewel Sita wore in her hair; in the ashoka grove she untied it and gave it to him, so that Rama would believe every word. Rama takes it, holds it against his chest, and weeps. Lakshmana stands beside him. To anyone else it's an ornament. To the two men looking at it, it's her.
screen: `HANUMAN OPENS HIS HAND.` → `A JEWEL FROM HER HAIR.` → `RAMA WEEPS.`

segments.voice: Rama knows the jewel at once. In Valmiki he says it came to Sita from her father, King Janaka, at their wedding, and that seeing it is almost like seeing her. Then he asks Hanuman again and again: what did she say? Tell me her exact words. So Hanuman passes on everything. Sita had sent a second token, and it was a story: the crow at Chitrakuta that kept attacking her, and the single blade of grass Rama sent after it as a weapon. Nobody else was there. A memory used as a password. And she sent a message with a deadline: she could hold on for one more month, and no longer. So the joy of seen arrives with a clock attached, and Rama's grief and resolve rise together. Why is this book called Sundara, beautiful? People give different answers, and nobody can say for certain which one Valmiki meant. But Hindu tradition treats the Sundara Kanda as a book of hope. It's recited on its own, start to finish, at home or in a temple, especially in hard times, because it's the stretch of the story where the lost is found and the long wait finally hears seen. And notice where it comes to rest: on a man asking to hear her words one more time. Devotees do the same with Rama's story. The Bhagavata Purana lists shravana, hearing the Lord's stories, first among the forms of devotion. Families who know every line of the Sundara Kanda still read it whole, again, because hearing it again is the prayer.
screen: `HER FATHER'S JEWEL.` · `A MEMORY AS A PASSWORD.` · `ONE MORE MONTH.` · `THE BOOK OF HOPE.` · then, large: `SHRAVANA: HEARING IT AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus keep a little shravana every day: a few verses read aloud, a bhajan, a recording of the Sundara Kanda playing while they cook. Try it now. If you pray, softly repeat the old Rama chant, Sri Rama, Jaya Rama, Jaya Jaya Rama, a few times, and simply listen to it. If you don't, bring to mind the words of someone you love, the way Rama asked for Sita's, and hear them once more.
Seen, Sita. The news that closes the Sundara Kanda, carried home with a jewel from her hair, a story only Rama would know, and one month on the clock.
Your line: shravana, hearing the story again is devotion. Tomorrow the war book, the Yuddha Kanda, begins. Until tomorrow.

Sundara Kanda.meaning: the fifth book of the Ramayana; sundara means beautiful

Chitrakuta.meaning: the forest mountain where Rama and Sita once lived

ashoka.meaning: a flowering tree; the grove where Sita was held

shravana.meaning: hearing the Lord's stories, a form of devotion
